module: Sexual and reproductive health — initial knowledge library
instructions: Educational information only, not for diagnosis or individualized medical recommendations. Do not store questions or sensitive personal data.

sources.name: CDC · Contraception and Birth Control Methods

cards.title: What is emergency contraception?
cards.answer: Emergency contraception can lower the chance of pregnancy after unprotected sex or contraceptive failure. Options include emergency contraceptive pills and the copper intrauterine device (IUD). It is not a substitute for regular contraception. Seek information and care as soon as possible.
aliases: what to do after unprotected sex
cards.follow_up: Would you like to learn about the available methods or the time window?

cards.title: How long do I have to act?
cards.answer: Emergency contraception is generally used within five days after unprotected sex, and prompt action matters. Timing and effectiveness differ by method. If this is a recent situation, contact a health service promptly rather than waiting to finish this educational activity.
aliases: how much time do I have
cards.follow_up: Would you like to compare emergency pills and the copper IUD?

cards.title: What emergency contraception options exist?
cards.answer: Options include levonorgestrel pills, ulipristal acetate pills, and the copper IUD. Certain combined oral contraceptive regimens are also used in some settings. The copper IUD is the most effective emergency method and must be inserted by a trained health professional. The appropriate option depends on timing and individual circumstances.
cards.follow_up: Would you like information about levonorgestrel, ulipristal, or the copper IUD?

cards.title: What is emergency levonorgestrel?
cards.answer: Levonorgestrel is used in emergency contraceptive pills. It should be taken as soon as possible; it can be used within five days, although it may be less effective after the first three days. It does not prevent sexually transmitted infections and is not a regular contraceptive method.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to compare levonorgestrel with ulipristal?

cards.title: What is ulipristal acetate?
cards.answer: Ulipristal acetate is a medicine used for emergency contraception within five days after unprotected sex. Between days three and five, it is generally more effective than levonorgestrel pills. Starting or resuming hormonal contraception after ulipristal requires specific guidance because of possible effects on effectiveness.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to know about restarting regular contraception?

cards.title: Can the copper IUD be used for emergency contraception?
cards.answer: Yes. A copper IUD inserted by a trained health professional within the appropriate time window can prevent pregnancy after unprotected sex. It is the most effective emergency contraceptive method and can be kept for ongoing contraception. Suitability and insertion require professional assessment.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to compare the copper IUD with emergency pills?

cards.title: Does emergency contraception cause abortion?
cards.answer: No. Emergency contraception prevents pregnancy; emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by preventing or delaying ovulation. They do not end an established pregnancy and are not abortion medication.
aliases: already pregnant and took morning after pill
cards.follow_up: Could you explain in your own words the difference between preventing and ending a pregnancy?

cards.title: Does emergency contraception always work?
cards.answer: No emergency contraceptive method is 100% effective. Effectiveness varies by method, timing, and other circumstances. The copper IUD is the most effective emergency option. If pregnancy remains a concern, consider a pregnancy test at the appropriate time and seek professional advice.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to know when to take a pregnancy test?

cards.title: What if the condom broke or slipped?
cards.answer: If a condom breaks or slips and pregnancy is possible, seek advice about emergency contraception promptly. An assessment of possible sexually transmitted infection exposure may also be relevant. If there may have been HIV exposure, some preventive treatment options require urgent medical evaluation.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to review emergency contraception timing or STI prevention?

cards.title: What if I missed my regular contraception?
cards.answer: Missing contraceptive pills or delaying another method can reduce protection. What to do depends on the exact method and timing. Emergency contraception may be considered in some situations. Check the instructions for your specific product and seek timely professional advice.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to learn which emergency contraception options exist?

cards.title: What if I vomited after taking an emergency pill?
cards.answer: Vomiting soon after an emergency contraceptive pill may affect absorption, and another dose might be needed. The relevant interval depends on the product and clinical guidance. Consult a health professional or pharmacist promptly for advice specific to the pill used.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to review other common side effects?

cards.title: What side effects may occur?
cards.answer: Emergency contraceptive pills can cause nausea, fatigue, or temporary changes in menstrual bleeding. These effects are generally mild. Severe abdominal pain, fainting, or very heavy bleeding warrants urgent medical assessment; CLARA cannot determine the cause.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to know when to consider a pregnancy test?

cards.title: When should I consider a pregnancy test?
cards.answer: Menstrual bleeding can change after emergency contraception. If there has been no menstrual bleeding within three weeks, guidance recommends taking a pregnancy test. If you experience severe pain, fainting, or heavy bleeding, seek medical care promptly.
aliases: late period after morning after pill
how to know if I am pregnant
cards.follow_up: Would you like to review signs that need medical attention?

cards.title: Can emergency contraception be used more than once?
cards.answer: Emergency contraception may be needed more than once, but it is not intended to replace regular contraception. If you need it repeatedly, a health professional can help you consider effective ongoing options that suit your preferences.
aliases: morning after pill twice in a month
cards.follow_up: Would you like to learn about regular contraception?

cards.title: How do I resume regular contraception afterward?
cards.answer: The guidance depends on the emergency pill used. Regular hormonal contraception can generally be started or resumed immediately after levonorgestrel; after ulipristal, guidance generally recommends waiting at least five days before starting or resuming hormonal methods. Backup condoms may be needed. Seek guidance about your specific product and circumstances.
aliases: restart contraception after morning after pill
start birth control after emergency pill
cards.follow_up: Would you like to review the differences between emergency and regular contraception?

cards.title: What contraceptive methods are available?
cards.answer: Options include long-acting reversible methods such as implants and IUDs; hormonal methods such as pills, injections, patches, and vaginal rings; barrier methods such as condoms; and permanent methods. No single option is best for everyone. Choosing a method should be informed and voluntary.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to compare duration, hormones, and STI protection?

cards.title: Which contraceptive methods are most effective?
cards.answer: Implants and IUDs are among the most effective reversible methods for preventing pregnancy. Pills, patches, vaginal rings, and injections can also be effective, but correct and timely use matters more. Condoms also help protect against many STIs. The right option depends on your needs and health circumstances.
aliases: what birth control do you recommend
cards.follow_up: Would you prefer to learn about long-acting or hormone-free methods?

cards.title: What is a contraceptive implant?
cards.answer: A contraceptive implant is a long-acting reversible method inserted beneath the skin of the arm by a trained professional. It releases a hormone to prevent pregnancy and is highly effective. It does not protect against STIs. Duration and details vary by product.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to compare the implant with an IUD?

cards.title: What is the difference between copper and hormonal IUDs?
cards.answer: Both are highly effective long-acting reversible methods inserted by a trained health professional. Copper IUDs contain no hormones; hormonal IUDs release a progestogen. Neither protects against STIs. Preferences, medical history, and possible side effects help guide the choice.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to review other hormone-free options?

cards.title: How do regular birth control pills work?
cards.answer: Birth control pills are hormonal methods used regularly. Some contain estrogen and a progestogen; others contain only a progestogen. Effectiveness depends on correct use. They do not protect against STIs, and some formulations require precautions depending on medical history. A qualified professional can help you compare choices.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to know about methods that do not require a daily pill?

cards.title: Which contraceptive options contain no hormones?
cards.answer: Hormone-free choices include the copper IUD and condoms. Other barrier and fertility-awareness methods also exist, but their effectiveness varies. Condoms help reduce the risk of STIs; a copper IUD does not.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to compare the copper IUD with condoms?

cards.title: What do condoms do?
cards.answer: When used correctly and consistently, condoms help prevent pregnancy and reduce the risk of many sexually transmitted infections, including HIV. They can be used with another contraceptive method for additional protection. They do not eliminate every risk.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to know what to do if a condom fails?

cards.title: What contraceptive methods can adolescents consider?
cards.answer: Adolescents need clear, respectful, nonjudgmental information about contraception. Age alone does not make one method universally best. Choosing a method depends on preferences, needs, and health circumstances and should involve appropriate professional guidance consistent with local rules. Condoms also help protect against many STIs.
aliases: best birth control for a teenager
cards.follow_up: Would you like to compare the main characteristics of contraceptive methods?

cards.title: Can contraception affect future fertility?
cards.answer: Fertility generally returns after stopping or removing reversible contraceptive methods, although timing varies by method and person. Emergency contraceptive pills do not harm future fertility. Individual concerns about fertility require professional assessment.
aliases: will birth control make me sterile
cards.follow_up: Would you like to learn about different reversible methods?

cards.title: What are sexually transmitted infections?
cards.answer: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) can spread through sexual contact, and many cause no noticeable symptoms. Prevention includes correct condom use, vaccinations where appropriate, testing, and access to care. Emergency contraception does not prevent STIs.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to know why testing may matter even without symptoms?

cards.title: What should I do after possible HIV exposure?
cards.answer: If you may have been exposed to HIV, seek urgent medical care. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) can lower the risk when clinically indicated and should start as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours after exposure. CLARA cannot determine whether PEP is needed.
cards.follow_up: Would you like general information about STI prevention and testing?

cards.title: What is HPV and how can it be prevented?
cards.answer: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is common and can spread through sexual contact. Some persistent infections are linked to cancers, including cervical cancer. Vaccination and recommended screening help prevent HPV-related disease. Condoms reduce, but do not eliminate, transmission risk.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to understand the difference between vaccination and screening?

cards.title: When should someone seek STI testing?
cards.answer: Many STIs have no symptoms. After possible exposure, symptoms, or concern, a health service can advise which tests may be useful and when to take them; timing depends on the infection and exposure. CLARA cannot interpret laboratory results or replace clinical assessment.
cards.follow_up: Would you like to learn general ways to reduce STI risk?

cards.title: What if sexual violence or coercion has occurred?
cards.answer: If you experienced sexual assault, seek medical care and specialist support as soon as possible. A health team can assess injuries, pregnancy prevention, infection prevention, and available support. You do not need to share intimate details with CLARA to receive general guidance. If you are in immediate danger, contact local emergency services or a trusted person.
cards.follow_up: Your safety and timely, respectful care come first.

cards.title: Which symptoms need urgent medical attention?
cards.answer: Severe abdominal pain, fainting, very heavy bleeding, or other serious symptoms require urgent medical evaluation. CLARA cannot diagnose their cause or rule out an emergency from a message. If you have severe symptoms, seek immediate medical care.
cards.follow_up: If you have severe symptoms, seek medical care now.
